lines.text: Chapter 1: The burger standard.
lines.say: Chapter one: the burger standard.

lines.text: Start with a simple question. If one thing is identical everywhere, shouldn't it cost about the same everywhere?
lines.say: Start with a simple question. If one thing is identical everywhere, shouldn't it cost about the same everywhere?

lines.text: Economists have a name for that idea: purchasing power parity, or PPP.
lines.say: Economists have a name for that idea: purchasing power parity, or P P P.

lines.text: PPP says that over the long run, exchange rates should drift toward the rate that makes the same basket of goods cost the same in every country.
lines.say: P P P says that over the long run, exchange rates should drift toward the rate that makes the same basket of goods cost the same in every country.

lines.text: Here's the logic. If gold were cheap in Mexico and pricey in America, traders would buy it in Mexico and sell it here.

lines.text: All that buying pushes up demand for pesos, and the price gap slowly closes.

lines.text: Real PPP research uses huge baskets with thousands of prices. That's slow, expensive, and honestly a little dull.

lines.text: So The Economist picked a basket of one: a Big Mac, sold in dozens of countries with basically the same recipe.

lines.text: The July 2026 edition covers 54 places, counting the US and treating the whole euro area as one.

lines.text: The Economist first ran the Big Mac index in September 1986. Economics writer Pam Woodall came up with it.

lines.text: The magazine itself calls it a lighthearted guide to whether currencies are at their correct level.

lines.text: It was meant as a fun way to explain a dry theory. Instead it gave the world a new word: burgernomics.

lines.text: Chapter 3: Doing the math.

lines.text: The whole index is two divisions. Grab a napkin.

lines.text: Step one: divide the local price by the US price. That gives you the implied exchange rate, the rate PPP says should exist.
lines.say: Step one: divide the local price by the US price. That gives you the implied exchange rate, the rate P P P says should exist.

lines.text: Step two: compare the implied rate with the real one. The gap is how over or undervalued the currency looks.

lines.text: Let's try Japan. In the July 2026 edition, a Big Mac in Japan costs 500 yen.

lines.text: So by the burger test, the yen is undervalued against the dollar by about half.

lines.text: So is the yen really worth twice what the market says? Not so fast.

lines.text: The big flaw: you can't ship a Big Mac across an ocean. Most of its price is local stuff that never crosses a border.

lines.text: There's a deeper pattern too. Richer countries have higher wages, so anything involving local labor tends to cost more there.

lines.text: That means poorer countries will almost always look undervalued on the raw index, even when nothing is wrong with their currency.

lines.text: One more limit. PPP is a long-run idea. A currency can look cheap or pricey for years, so the index isn't a forecast.

lines.text: So why should an American care about a burger in Tokyo? Because exchange rates show up in prices you pay.

lines.text: Exchange rates reach Americans in three main ways.

lines.text: Travel first. At the July 2026 survey, one dollar bought about 162 yen, so dollars stretched a long way in Japan.

post.title: A Big Mac is $9.04 in Switzerland and $3.08 in Japan. Here's what that says about money.

post.yt_desc:
In The Economist's July 2026 Big Mac index, a Big Mac costs $9.04 in Switzerland, $6.22 in the US and $3.08 in Japan. This video explains purchasing power parity in plain words, the index's history since 1986, and the exact two-step math that makes the Swiss franc look 45.4% overvalued and the yen 50.4% undervalued. We cover the euro area, Britain, Mexico, China and India, the GDP-adjusted version, where the burger test breaks (rent, wages, taxes), and how exchange rates reach an American's wallet through travel, imports and exports. The next edition is expected in early 2027.

News and education, not financial advice.
